column1: A market simulation engine already exists in C# and the BTM engine must be built around it.
Three workloads have different needs: the engine, optimisation, and model fitting.
The engine workload needs throughput, low allocation pressure, strong typing, and to sit next to the existing simulator.
Optimisation needs a MILP solver, and Gurobi is the intended choice but is deliberately not fixed yet.
Model fitting is research work, iterated far more often than the engine, and the tooling for it is not C#.
C# on the current .NET LTS is used for everything in the runtime pipeline, with no polyglot runtime.
The existing simulator is the anchor, and splitting the hot path across a process boundary would destroy backtest throughput.
The solver sits behind IOptimizationBackend.
The Planner constructs a solver-independent MilpModel of variables, linear terms, PWL segments, epigraph constraints, indicator constraints and SOS2 sets, and the backend translates it.
Gurobi, HiGHS and a pure-LP relaxation backend are all expressible through IOptimizationBackend.
Model fitting is offline and out of process, and the engine consumes artefacts rather than a live model.
An artefact is a versioned, content-hashed file of coefficients, breakpoints or lookup surfaces with a declared schema, loaded through the Belief cold tier like any other data.
A model needed at runtime is either exported to a form C# can evaluate natively — a PWL table, a tree ensemble, a small tensor — or it does not go in the hot path.
Separating fitting a model from using a model is what makes model versions replayable in backtest.
There is no ONNX or Python interop in the tick loop.
A model too complex to export is too complex to be in the tick loop.
IOptimizationBackend must be designed against the union of what the ADR-010 tiers need, so that switching backends does not silently change the formulation.
Backend conformance is a test level: the same model solved by two backends must agree on objective value within tolerance.
Hot-path C# discipline is mandatory: struct-of-arrays, Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T>, ArrayPool<T>, no LINQ in the tick loop, and no per-slot object allocation.
A year-long backtest with scenario ensembles is allocation-bound long before it is CPU-bound.
Cross-process serialisation of scenario ensembles per tick dominates the solve time in backtest.
Calling the solver directly ties the formulation to one vendor's API idioms and makes it impossible to run the LP-relaxation oracle used for gap measurement.
Live ML inference in the tick is non-deterministic across library versions, unreplayable, and a source of latency variance nobody can attribute.
Real operation has at least four rhythms with different information sets and different irreversibility: accounting periods, a slow value-function loop, market gates, and event-driven intraday ticks.
Gate times, product definitions and auction structures change by regulation and by venue.
The four clocks are C_accounting, C_slow, C_gate and C_tick.
All calendar and product structure is data, loaded from a versioned MarketCalendar artefact.

The MarketCalendar includes gate closure times, auction schedules, product block definitions including aFRR block length and symmetry, delivery period definitions, exchange holidays, tick and lot sizes, and the Hochlastzeitfenster table per DSO per year.
The calendar artefact is part of the backtest manifest and is replayed with the run.
A backtest of 2024 uses the 2024 calendar, not today's.
The tzdata version is pinned and recorded in the run manifest, because civil time itself is versioned data.
A regulatory or venue change is a data change plus a test fixture, not a code change.
HLZF windows and §19(2) thresholds are republished per DSO per year.
The engine cannot hardcode 96 slots per day, and every horizon is expressed in SlotSpan derived from the calendar.
DST days are test fixtures, not edge cases discovered in production.
Backtests across a rule change are honest because the engine sees the rules that applied at the time.
The calendar artefact must itself be validated for monotone gates, no overlapping blocks, and every delivery slot covered by exactly one product block.
The calendar indirection costs an indirection on every time question.
Gate times as constants change, and a wrong gate time silently makes a backtest optimistic, which is the worst possible failure because it looks like alpha.
A single tick loop with an isGateTime branch conflates information sets, so the Planner cannot express that one decision is binding and another is not.
Using the system timezone is non-reproducible across machines and across tzdata releases.
Energy optimisation code is dominated by two silent bug classes: sign-frame confusion and unit confusion.
Sign-frame and unit confusion both produce plausible numbers, neither throws, and both survive code review.
Where the peak term is a max and the reserve term is a curve, a sign error does not merely scale the answer but inverts the strategy.
The two sign frames genuinely coexist because markets price the battery's export while §19 StromNEV prices the site's import.
Quantities are distinct value types rather than double, implemented as readonly record structs wrapping a double with no implicit conversions between frames or units.
Arithmetic on typed quantities is defined only where it is dimensionally meaningful.
The minimum typed-quantity set is BatteryPowerKw, PoiPowerKw, LoadKw, PvKw, ReserveMw, EnergyKwh, EnergyPrice, CapacityPrice, PeakPrice, Money, Efficiency, SocFraction, SlotId and SlotSpan.
There is exactly one sanctioned conversion between frames, p_poi = load − pv − p_batt, in one place.
There is exactly one kW to MW conversion per direction, at the market adapter.
The bridge between frames becomes a single, heavily tested function rather than a sign flip scattered through the code.
Serialisation must handle the typed wrappers, and contracts declare the underlying primitive plus a unit field so that a mismatch is a schema failure rather than a runtime surprise.
Typed quantities cost some ceremony in arithmetic-heavy inner loops.
The hot numeric kernels — scenario reduction and PWL evaluation — operate on raw ReadOnlySpan<double> inside a typed façade.
Type safety belongs at the boundary where errors actually occur, not inside a loop the JIT must vectorise.
No contract field is a bare double without a declared unit.
Naming discipline instead of types relies on reviewers and does not survive refactoring or agent-authored code.
A units library's generality costs allocation and readability, while the fixed set of typed quantities is small and closed.
A single signed POI-frame variable everywhere makes market-facing code read backwards and makes the efficiency split awkward.
A backtest is only worth running if it is impossible for the engine to have used information it did not have at the time.
Lookahead leakage produces excellent backtests and losing live performance.

Lookahead leakage is usually introduced by an innocuous convenience: a silently revised forecast series, a settlement value stamped with the delivery time rather than the publication time, or a latest-available lookup with no as_of.
The full information set — order book deltas for every intraday product, ensemble forecasts, aFRR data, meter data — cannot be resident in memory and does not need to be.
A tick needs a window, not a history.
Loading what you need with careful timestamps is slow because the access pattern is unpredictable and unsafe because correctness depends on discipline.
Every fact is stored with valid_time, the slot the fact describes, and knowledge_time, when the engine could first have known it.
The only read API is Get(series, validRange, asOf: knowledgeTime) returning a column slice.
There is no read overload without asOf and no API that returns a fact with knowledge_time greater than asOf.
The asOf filter is applied inside the storage layer against an index, not by the caller.
Lookahead safety is structural: to leak, a developer or an agent would have to change the storage layer rather than merely forget a filter.
Revisions are appended and never updated in place.
A price series revised three times has three rows with the same valid_time and three different knowledge_times.
asOf selects the latest row at or before the read time, which is exactly what the engine saw.
The Belief store has three tiers: cold, warm and hot.

The cold tier is immutable Parquet partitioned by (series, source, date), holds everything at source fidelity including raw order-book deltas and derived feature artefacts, is permanent, and is accessed by offline calibration and by the cold-start of a replay.
The warm tier is memory-mapped columnar frames, LRU-evicted, one frame per (series, day), holding what the current replay position needs for the session, accessed by the Belief cursor.

The hot tier is a preallocated struct-of-arrays window covering [t, t + H_hot], holding only the series and slots the current tick's contract requires, refilled in place each tick, accessed by Valuation via C1.
The hot window is bounded by the horizon, not by history.
Belief memory is O(#series × H_hot × #scenarios) regardless of backtest length.
Nothing about a multi-year backtest's memory footprint grows with time.
The warm tier is memory-mapped so the OS page cache does the eviction work, and sequential replay is exactly the access pattern page caching is good at.
A BeliefSnapshot is an immutable value carrying (asOf, revisionId) and read-only ReadOnlyMemory<T> views over the hot window's buffers.
The hot window's buffers are contractually immutable for the duration of the tick.
A BeliefSnapshot is cheap to create, cannot be mutated, and is content-addressed by the hash of the inputs that produced it.
A snapshot may carry a read-only view over a buffer frozen for the tick, but may not carry a handle — anything advanceable, refreshable, or aliasing state another component can mutate.
A materialised value form, BeliefSnapshotRecord, exists for seam recording and satisfies C0's serialisability requirement.
BeliefSnapshot and BeliefSnapshotRecord carry identical content and hash identically.

Anything expensive to compute and reused — fill-probability surfaces, price-impact curves, scenario ensembles, activation-probability models — is computed once offline, written to the cold tier keyed by FeatureSpecHash, and read back as data.
Backtests never recompute derived features.
A backtest can never silently use a different feature definition than the one recorded.
The raw order book stays cold and is never materialised in the hot path.

What crosses C1 is the derived quantity the Planner actually needs: for a given product and slot, a compact representation of achievable volume as a function of limit price and of the probability of fill.
The raw order book exists for calibration and for high-fidelity replay, not for the tick loop.
Lookahead auditing is a cheap, decisive test: run a backtest with all facts having knowledge_time > t replaced by garbage and assert bit-identical results.
If any component peeks, the garbage-replacement run diverges.
Every data source must declare its publication semantics, and a series that cannot answer when the engine knew a fact is quarantined rather than guessed.
Revisions being first-class gives Settlement the ability to distinguish being wrong from the data having been later corrected.
Storage cost is higher than a last-value-wins store, and this is the correct trade.
The ingestion layer is more work than it looks and must be built before anything above it.
A single-temporal store with careful queries is correctness by discipline, whose failure mode is a backtest that looks like alpha.
Keeping everything in memory does not survive order-book data or multi-year runs.
Recomputing features per tick is slow and silently version-drifts between a research run and a production run.
A database in the hot path introduces query latency and non-determinism, while a memory-mapped columnar frame is orders of magnitude faster and exactly reproducible.
